chapter_theme: Natrinai 181 to 200: shore and hill love in short scenes, a sparrow's evening and a moon called to witness, mothers left behind by eloping daughters, friends who press for marriage through confinement and harvest, and Kolli's god-made figure used to measure a girl's beauty as both danger and protection.

181.reading: The friend watches the evening: a sparrow cock that had lodged with companions in other fields comes back drenched, and the hen, guarding her small chicks bright as iingai flowers, first bars him from the nest, then, seeing his wet back, gives him a place beside her and calls him in with a softened heart; because that helpless, bewildering evening had come, the chariot came, its garlanded horses cutting the cool crops, and the beauty of this girl's brow is saved.
181.nuance: Line 2 lets the cock's night away be read as a stay with another mate, which would make the hen's relenting a lesson in forgiveness; the friend does not press it, and the poem only needs the evening return. The horses 'cutting the cool crops' shows the chariot taking the shortest way, through the fields.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றிப் புகுந்தது கண்ட தோழி மகிழ்ந்து உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: drizzle and evening are the rains and hour of mullai

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of the heroine as இவள், as if aloud to herself

iraicchi.act: the hen, after barring the nest, pities her drenched mate and calls him in beside her and the chicks
iraicchi.sense: the wife who waited will take back the man who comes home at the rainy evening, and the house will close round him

182.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend tells the girl the moon has set and darkness has come, and the mother of great wealth who guards her, doll-like, in the wide house that looks like a painting, sleeps; let us go softly, see him, and embrace his good chest close as one takes up a fine jewel that was lost, for he has come alone like a great tusker left by the keepers above and below, out in the cold.
182.nuance: The proposal is addressed to the girl but aimed at the listener: the riskiness of the night, the sleeping guardian and his lonely state as a keeperless elephant all tell him that secret visits cannot go on, which is how the friend presses for marriage.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட்டிப்ப தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமை அறிந்த தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: a night meeting in secret love is kurinji's uri

comparisons.tenor: the wide house of the girl's family
the embrace of the man after long waiting

183.reading: The friend tells the shore lord, who is leaving with the marriage put off, that even the salt merchants' going is painful, who bring white paddy from their own country, cry the price of salt from another, drive long lines of carts across moonlit sand and move with their kin; he is foolish, for evenings with the cruel wind now hold the loneliness of his absence, and he does not consider that she will not live, like a neythal in shallow water trampled by a white heron that has fed on shoals of fish.
183.nuance: The salt merchants are strangers who leave with their whole household and still sadden the shore; he leaves without taking anyone, which is the friend's point about marriage. The heron has fed full and the flower is trampled in passing: the harm is careless, not cruel.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை வைத்துப் பிரியும் தலைவற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: salt, heron and neythal of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the girl who will not live

occasion.words: வரைவிடை வைத்துப் பிரியும் தலைவற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

184.reading: The mother says she had one daughter, and she too went yesterday with a sharp-speared youth across the hard waste of the great hills; you tell me to bear my grief, wise ones, but how can that be, when my heart burns at the very thought, seeing the bright nochchi and the raised terrace where my lovely girl played, she who was like the figure in the eye's pupil learning to walk.
184.nuance: 'One daughter' is the whole argument against consolation: there is no other child to turn to. The pupil image is doubled, the dearest thing in the eye and a tiny figure only just learning to walk, so the girl is remembered as a toddler at the moment she has gone off as a bride.

colophon.thurai: மனை மருட்சி

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's flight with her lover across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: she answers the neighbours who console her, calling them அறிவுடையீரே

185.reading: The man says that if you will not even look on the helpless pain of passion grown past bearing, then she, like the finely wrought figure a god painted on the western face of the famous high Kolli of Porayan, where the bards' gift horses with worn hooves climb the small rock path and suppliants go up without tiring, where honeycombs hang among kaanthal clusters, has plotted my death; shall I grieve?
185.nuance: நல்காய், 'you do not grant', suits the second alternative better, the friend who keeps him off. The girl is a figure painted by a god: a made, divine beauty, so the plot to kill is hers and not hers; and the long praise of Porayan's open-handed hill sets her refusal against a lord who turns no suppliant away.

colophon.thurai: பாங்கற்குத் தலைவன் சொல்லியது சேட்படுக்கும் தோழிக்குத் தலைவன் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal, honeycomb and the high hill

186.reading: The woman tells her wasting friend that the road their beloved took runs through a scorched, drought-struck forest where the great elephant, the rock springs not filling, stretches its rough trunk, scoops up water and runs to his mate, and the old lizard, its colour changed by summer, climbs the tall yaa bent like the end of a bard's lute; he went with a great-hearted wish to strive for others, held by the lovely bond of wealth.
186.nuance: The roles are reversed: the wife defends the absent husband to the friend, and justifies the journey by its purpose, wealth sought to be given to others, not by its gain.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தோழிக்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: scorched forest and summer drought

comparisons.tenor: the bent body of the old lizard

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon makes the friend the one who has wasted; the heroine comforts her

iraicchi.act: in the drought the tusker scoops water from the rock spring and runs with it to his mate
iraicchi.sense: even on that road a male's first care is his mate, so the man crossing it holds his wife in mind and works for her

187.reading: The girl, to herself, watches the evening close in, the neythal folding, shadows running east, the sun reddening at the hill and the many-flowered shore grove going quiet, as his chariot is yoked with ringing bells and its back vanishes while she stands worshipping in full desire; she asks what will become, with the town, of the grove where they played and laughed with the shore lord of the bee-humming garland and bright curved ornaments.
187.nuance: The worry is about the place, not the man: 'with the town' (ஊரொடு) fears that the grove of their meetings will become the town's talk. Every sign of the hour is also a sign of closing, the flower, the shadows, the grove, and then the chariot's back.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பகற்குறி வந்து மீள்வானது செலவு நோக்கி தலைமகள் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: sunset on the shore grove

188.reading: The friend tells the lord of the sky-touching hill, where on a wet slope the banana's curved sheath has put out a sharp closed bud that touches the broad kaanthal petal as women's soft fingers touch their bright bangles, that had the girl known well then that even good fortune comes with harm, her bamboo-like shoulders would not now be wasting.
188.nuance: The banana bud touching the kaanthal is a near miss for ullurai (the man's approach to the girl), but it gives one pair only, so it stays scene. The maxim of line 6, good bringing harm with it, turns their happy daytime meetings into the cause of her wasting, which is why the friend refuses them.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal and banana on the hill slope

comparisons.tenor: the banana bud touching the kaanthal petal

189.reading: The friend says that though he, who has no one but us and loves us, has not yet come, will he really go off in the ships of the Ganges before the hard-to-anger god of the Chenniyar, where the heron's sweet voice sounds like a plucked string of the small lute; what can they be doing, who crossed the lovely forest of withered branches where the wood-dove cock that broke free of the cruel hunter's net now fears even the spider's thread on the bough?
189.nuance: The dove that escaped the net and now shies at a cobweb is not iraicchi under the rule (it fears, it does not do what a lover does or should do); it gives the road its mood of fright after danger. Lines 2 to 5 are best taken as a reassuring question: he will not go as far as the Ganges.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: a forest of dead branches

190.reading: The man tells his heart to suffer now, the heart that delighted in the few words and coral-mouthed smile of the young girl with eyes cool and frightened as a netted deer's, whose lovely shoulders took a beauty like Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan of the spotted spear, giver lavish as rain in his joy, lord of the fine chariot and fragrant garland, where neythal blooms among the paddy in fields of toddy.
190.nuance: The heart is blamed for its pleasure: 'suffer now' because it once rejoiced. The fields of Arkkadu are marutham, so a kurinji love is measured by a lowland town; the colophon's three alternatives fit because the poem names no occasion.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் ஆற்றானாகி நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது அல்லகுறிப்பட்டு மீள்வான் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம் இடைச் சுரத்துச் சென்று தலைமகள் நலம் உள்ளி மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's heart caught by a girl in secret love

occasion.words: இடைச் சுரத்துச் சென்று தலைமகள் நலம் உள்ளி மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறியதூஉம்

191.reading: With the man listening, the friend says that in their lovely hamlet fenced with kandal, where the honeyed bright clusters of the small-flowered njaazhal fall lightly on the spotted breasts of the sand dolls the girls shape on the long sand, the town has raised talk, saying a chariot came at night, and among them all mother looked at me; if I do not pick the blue mundakam tomorrow there will be nothing to adorn her, and harder still will be his chariot coming to the fragrant shore grove and going away empty.
191.nuance: The confinement is announced without naming it: if the girls cannot go out for flowers tomorrow, the man's chariot will find the grove empty. The flowers dropping on the sand doll's breasts recall the girls' play that is about to end.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாக செறிப்பு அறிவுறுப்பான் வேண்டிச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: njaazhal, kandal and mundakam of the shore

192.reading: The man tells the girl, who wept and complained at length asking why he comes in love by the long mountain path where the blood-thirsty tiger watches the young elephant and rain-dark bears graze daily like the Puzhiyar's flocks in the dense grove, that when he comes thinking of her fine beauty, like the new figure the spirits set on the western hill of Kolli rich in jackfruit, shining like young sunlight of spreading rays, the mountain path itself becomes his safety.
192.nuance: Her fear lists the dangers, his answer does not deny them: the thought of her is a charm (ஏமம்) that makes the road safe. The comparison to a figure set up by spirits gives her beauty the protective power of a shrine.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி மறுக்கப்பட்டு ஆற்றானாய தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: bears, jackfruit and the hill path

193.reading: The woman asks the great cold north wind, which roams the new-wet flooded fields, mixes drops into the soft-tipped new flowers of the iingai with round buds the colour of molten lac, and endlessly hugs her dark back, whether she has done it any harm: her lover, who loosened the bright bangles of her shoulders, has left for hard-won wealth, so let it not torment one who sits alone in a corner in great sorrow.
193.nuance: The wind 'embraces her back' (இரும் புறம் தழூஉம்): the only embrace she has is the cold one, and she reproaches it as if it were a person doing a wrong.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: separation for wealth; the cold season is the season of her waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks to the north wind

194.reading: The friend, with the hill lord listening, asks what return they can make, not only to the lordly elephant with high tusks and trailing trunk that moves with his mate beside their soft-mouthed calf, but to the small green parrot that can no longer take the great ears of millet the sickle has seized, since thanks to them they played with the hill lord in a hidden corner of dense trees that even the monkey does not know, leaving the lone guard platform on the rock deserted.
194.nuance: The thanks are ironic and the news is plain: the millet is reaped, so the girls' guarding and their meetings in the field are over. Why the elephant is thanked is not said; it may be the danger that kept others off the field.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகச் செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: millet, parrot and guard platform

iraicchi.act: the tusker goes about together with his mate beside their calf
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord should keep the girl as the tusker keeps his mate and young, in a household, now that the field meetings have ended

195.reading: The friend tells the lord of the gentle shore, where an otter cub gorges on fat fish of the dark backwater and sleeps in the thillai thicket, that it is cruel not to show grace: she has seen that the eyes of the girl he loves weep wet, like the many-petalled unclosing neythal of Thondi, shore of clamouring birds, tossing in water when the reapers' sharp sickles strike it.

colophon.thurai: களவின்கண் நெடுங்காலம் வந்தொழுக ஆற்றாளாயின தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, otter and thillai of the shore

ullurai.tenor: the lover who enjoys the girl and rests at ease

pairs.situation: he takes his pleasure of the girl in secret love
he then rests content and does not hasten to marry her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a creature of the backwater in a neythal poem without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

196.reading: The woman, alone with the full moon, tells it that since it has nobility and rectitude, a moon of many crystal rays and fresh white light as if scooped from milk, which no ladder reaches, and since no world can hide from it, it should show where they live who hide from her; or else, shrinking little by little like her shoulders that lost their beauty, it will waste, as a witness that knows and lies must.
196.nuance: She argues like a litigant: the moon sees everything, so it is a witness, and a witness who knows and keeps silent is a liar; its monthly waning is then the punishment she wishes on it, the same wasting her own shoulders suffer.

colophon.thurai: நெட்டிடை கழிந்து பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த காலத்து ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகள் திங்கள் மேலிட்டுத் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a night lament with no land; irangal decides

197.reading: The friend tells the girl, whose bangles slip, whose brow is overrun with pallor like peerkku flowers and whose eyes hold cool tears, not to sink saying her life will surely wane: in his good hill country the moving clouds now crawl, flashing like the gold bangles on the small forearms of young women who bring bee-visited new flowers to the bathing ghat, thundering like a troop of sweet-voiced drums, massed like the many shields of kings scaling forts.
197.nuance: The colophon is paalai, but the poem's comfort is the rainy season on his hills, the time a man returns; the three similes move from women's bangles to drums to shields, as if the clouds were an army coming home.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளைத் தோழி ஆற்றுவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the coming rains, lightning and thunder are mullai's season of waiting

occasion.words: வரைவு நீட ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளைத் தோழி ஆற்றுவித்தது

198.reading: The woman who followed the girl into the waste tells those she meets on the forest path of tall yaa and omai that her daughter passed this way yesterday, and her eyes are sunk in tears; she describes the girl, with spotted waist, fine bright teeth, few bangles and thick hair, learns that this is the town of the youth's father, a strong bowman whose arrows do not miss and who gives freely in his joy, and blesses them: I am the one who bore her; may your name prosper.
198.nuance: The search ends in a blessing rather than a demand: finding herself at the house of the youth's father, the woman gives the girl up and wishes the family well.

colophon.thurai: பின் சென்ற செவிலி இடைச் சுரத்துக் கண்டார்க்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: following the eloped daughter across the waste

199.reading: The girl tells her friend that each time the grieving white heron in its nest in the swollen frond of the tall palmyra on the high dune cries in the dense midnight, she melts, her heart breaking inside like a mire; she lives on only until she meets the body-touching embrace of the shore lord, where the lamps of fishers in curved boats that hunt fierce sharks, strung out on their bent lines and scattered by the wind, twinkle slowly like stars in the blue sky.
199.nuance: She answers the friend's comfort by refusing it: she 'lives' (உளெனே) only provisionally. The heron only cries, so it carries mood, not iraicchi; the twinkling lamps of the fishers are the lights of his shore seen from hers.

colophon.thurai: வன்புறை எதிரழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: palmyra, shark and fishers of the shore

200.reading: The friend, while the bard who came as go-between listens, calls the old-tongued potter who, wearing a nochchi garland of bright clusters like a chaplet of grain ears, cries the festival through the long wide street that lies like a river, and asks him to cry this too in the pond town of sweet fields thick with water-lily: the troubles this bard of the hand-plucked lute has caused are many, so let the women with fine teeth and broad hips guard themselves from his lie-wrapped crooked words.
200.nuance: The insult is public by design: the town crier is asked to proclaim the bard a liar, so the refusal reaches the husband through the whole street rather than through his messenger.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளது குறிப்பு அறிந்து வாயிலாகப் புக்க பாணன் கேட்ப குயவனைக் கூவி இங்ஙனம் சொல்லாயோ என்று குயவற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: refusing the husband's go-between in the field town

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

occasion.words: குயவனைக் கூவி இங்ஙனம் சொல்லாயோ என்று குயவற்குச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: she addresses the potter who cries the festival

links.note: Both men measure the girl by a divine figure on Kolli: in 185 the figure-like girl has plotted his death; in 192 thinking of her figure-like beauty makes the beast-haunted path safe.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kolli image proves double-edged: the same god-made beauty is a killing power when the girl or her friend refuses him and a protecting charm when she fears for him, so its force depends on which way her favour runs.

links.note: The figure painted by a god on the western face of Porayan's Kolli measures the girl in both; in the Kuruntokai the friend uses it, in Natrinai 185 the lover.
links.teaches: The friend uses the Kolli figure to plead that so innocent a girl can bring no harm to the town, while the lover uses the same figure to say she is killing him; the shared image shows the figure stood for a beauty both harmless in itself and dangerous to the one who sees it.

links.note: Both compare the girl's beauty to Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan: Natrinai 190 at its height, which the lover's heart rejoiced in; Kuruntokai 258 as it wastes under gossip.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems use Azhisi's rich town as a fixed standard of the girl's beauty and show both ends of it, the lover's delight and the friend's report of its ruin, so that one patron's town served the poets as a measure of beauty gained and lost.

links.note: The neythal of Thondi stands for the girl's eyes in both: in 195 the flower cut by reapers tossing in water, in Akananuru 290 the flower whose sapphire beauty has turned to gold.
links.teaches: The pair shows that Thondi's neythal was a set measure for the beloved's eyes, and that two poets spoiled it in two ways: by tears, the cut flower tossing in water, and by pallor, the blue turned to gold.

links.note: In both the separated woman speaks to the moon about the man who is gone: the Kural asks it not to set so she may see him; Natrinai 196 asks it to show where he hides.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into one blessing and plea a scene the Natrinai poem argues at length: the moon sees all worlds, so its silence is a witness's lie and its waning the punishment, which shows how much reasoning lies behind the Kural's single request.

links.note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother says the girl did not think of the nochchi or her playmates when she left; in Natrinai 184 the mother cannot bear to see the nochchi and the terrace where the girl played.
links.teaches: The pair shows the same household shrub on both sides of the elopement: forgotten by the daughter who has gone, and unbearable to the mother who stays, so the left-behind play things measure how unequal the parting is.

links.note: Kural 212 says wealth earned by effort exists to do good to the worthy; in Natrinai 186 the wife says her husband crossed the waste for wealth with a heart that strives for others.
links.teaches: The wife in the poem defends a painful separation with the Kural's ethic of earning in order to give, so the household rule appears here as the reason that made the paalai journey honourable in her eyes.

links.note: Kural 211: duty seeks no return, and the world makes none to the rain. Natrinai 194: the friend asks what return (கைம்மாறு) they can make to the elephant and the parrot.
links.teaches: The friend applies the Kural's word for repayment to beasts who helped without meaning to, the parrot that raided the millet and so kept the girls in the field, so her mock gratitude turns the rule of unrepayable benefit into a teasing way of announcing that the meetings are over.

links.note: Both poems call on the potter of the town: Purananuru 228 to make the burial urn for a dead Chola king; Natrinai 200 as the crier who proclaims festivals, asked to proclaim the bard a liar.
links.teaches: Taken together, the potter appears as the town's public servant for both its funerals and its festivals, and the friend's commission parodies the solemn address to him by making the crier's voice carry a domestic quarrel.

197: line 4 is a repaired TSCII leftover (தேயர் is read as printed), as show flags.
198: the colophon makes the speaker the foster mother (செவிலி), but line 12 says ஈன்றேன் யானே, 'I bore her'; the speaker is coded sevili as the colophon has it.
186: the colophon says the heroine speaks to a friend who has wasted (மெலிந்த தோழிக்கு); it is copied as it stands.
